chapter_theme: Greatness of character: it renounces when the season of giving and loving has passed, sees home and its supports as passing, and keeps giving even in decline. Its faults show more than others' crimes, it stays unshaken by slander, and it feeds others before itself.
structure_note: 181 to 183 speak of renunciation and impermanence; 184 to 190 describe the great in their giving, their visibility and their steadiness.

181.reading: We can no longer give, youth has gone far off, and those who once loved us no longer think of us; it seems the right course is to give up the craving that says 'we will love and prosper' and to leave.
181.nuance: The reasons for renouncing here are practical and even rueful, not doctrinal. Mudaliar specifies the departure as going into renunciation, and the loved ones as women.

182.reading: Fools think 'we found contentment by taking to home life; here we are complete', and go on heedless; those who see that such supports only seem to stand and do not last never grieve.
182.nuance: Mudaliar allows பரிவது to mean either grieving or desiring; Pope takes the second. The verse targets complacency in home life; whether it condemns home life itself depends on the reader.

positions.position: The supports that fail are the attachments of household life.

183.reading: Without confusion sow the seed for the next life, and live wisely without being brought low; for standing just where it stands the body changes its colour without any cause, and many ills arise.
183.nuance: Mudaliar supplies the subject: it is the body whose youth and qualities change unbidden. Pope's version speaks more vaguely of 'the changing hue of things'.

184.reading: They say a spring-fed well, even in a season of scant rain, serves the town that draws from it; the great keep their duty of giving even when they have declined, as others do not even when they have prospered.
184.nuance: Only the Tamil and Pope are available for this quatrain; neither commentary is aligned to it.

185.reading: Like a river that poured out abundant water to feed the world and, when dry, still yields water from springs dug in its bed, the generous who gave to many still give to a few when ruined, and do what ought to be done.

186.reading: Lord of the high hills, a fault in the great shows like a brand on a great white bull, while the small may do things as cruel as killing that bull and not one of them is noticed.
186.nuance: This is an observation about visibility, not a defence of the small. The high standard applies because the great are watched.

187.reading: Intimacy with the inherently mean brings grief for as long as it lasts, but even enmity with the wise, who would not want harmful things even in jest, brings dignity.

188.reading: Be gentler than the gentle good; toward foes, be a terror that Death itself would fear; toward the false, utterly false; toward the good, goodness itself: let these be one's bounds.
188.nuance: A policy of matching each person in kind. Pope reads சலவர் as the persistent, to be met with persistence; Mudaliar reads them as liars, to be met with lies. Mudaliar also notes that others construe the verse differently.

positions.position: Toward liars, one should be wholly a speaker of lies.

189.reading: Though someone hurries in and tries to confuse them with cruel slander, the pure in heart stay unshaken, with no division in their mind, like the bright flame inside a lamp.
189.nuance: The flame is steady because the lamp shields it; the image suggests an inner composure that slander cannot reach.

190.reading: The worthy daily give in charity the food served first and eat what is served after; that eating removes the three faults and keeps them from sorrow as long as life lasts.
190.nuance: Shanmuganar names the three faults as desire, anger and delusion. Pope leaves them unnamed, and no Mudaliar gloss is aligned.

links.note: 1050 says the destitute who do not renounce merely consume salt and gruel. 181 has someone who can no longer give conclude that renunciation is the fitting course.
331 calls taking the impermanent for permanent the lowest understanding; 182 gives the example of the householder who thinks himself settled for good.

46 asks what one gains by leaving a virtuous household life for the ascetic way. 182 calls those content in home life fools and praises those who see its supports as passing. The conflict holds on Mudaliar's reading, where the failing supports are household attachments themselves; if 182 targets only heedlessness, the two are compatible.
Both urge good deeds now because the body may fail without warning: 335 before the death-hiccup stops the tongue, 183 because the body changes without cause.
Both use a village water source for the generous: 215 compares a wise man's wealth to a full town tank, 184 compares the great in decline to a spring-fed well that still serves in drought.
218 says those who know their duty do not slacken in serving others even when they have no means; 184 says the great keep giving in decline.
Consecutive water images for giving in decline: a spring-fed well in 184, a dry riverbed that yields to digging in 185.
Both end with செய்வர் செயற்பாலவை. In 153 the poor worthy do their duty within their means; in 185 the once-rich keep doing it after ruin, for fewer people.
955: even when what they can give has shrunk, an old family keeps its nature. 185 says the same of the ruined giver who still gives to a few.
957 says a fault in the well-born stands out like the moon's spot; 186 says the same with a brand on a white bull, and adds that the crimes of the small go unseen.
816: being a stranger to the wise is ten million times better than intimacy with a fool. 187 goes further: even enmity with the wise brings dignity, while intimacy with the mean brings grief.

987 asks what worth is for if it cannot do good even to those who do harm. 188 says to meet foes with terror and the false with falseness. The conflict is direct on Mudaliar's reading of சலவர் as liars; on Pope's reading the third clause is milder, but the clause on foes still conflicts.
830 advises friendship of the face, not the heart, with a foe who turns friendly. 188 likewise answers each person in their own coin rather than with uniform goodness.
360 says suffering ends when desire, anger and delusion perish. On Shanmuganar's reading of the three faults, 190 offers a practice that removes them: feeding others before oneself.
227: hunger does not touch one who habitually shares food. 190 says sharing the first-served food keeps the worthy from sorrow till the end.
